question: Why can two magnetic field lines NEVER intersect or cross each other at any point in space?
options: Because at the point of intersection, a compass needle would have to point in two different directions simultaneously, which is physically impossible
Because magnetic field lines are electrostatic in nature
Because magnetic field lines repel each other with electrostatic Coulomb forces
Because the magnetic field becomes zero wherever lines cross
explanation: The direction of the magnetic field at any point is represented by the tangent to the field line at that point (the direction a magnetic north pole points). If two lines crossed, there would be two tangents, meaning two different field directions at a single location, which is physically impossible.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.1 Magnetic Field and Field Lines

subtopic: Magnetic Field Properties: Continuity of Field Loops
question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the direction of magnetic field lines outside and inside a permanent bar magnet?
options: Outside: South to North; Inside: North to South
Outside: North to South; Inside: Field is strictly zero
Field lines begin at the North pole and terminate permanently at the South pole
Outside: North to South; Inside: South to North (forming continuous closed loops)
explanation: By convention, magnetic field lines emerge from the North pole and enter the South pole outside the magnet. Inside the magnet, the direction of field lines is from its South pole to its North pole. Thus, magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops.

North Pole
East Pole

subtopic: Magnetic Force: Maximum vs Zero Force Conditions
question: Under what orientation between a straight current-carrying conductor and an external magnetic field is the mechanical force acting on the conductor ZERO?
options: When the conductor is perpendicular (90°) to the magnetic field
When the conductor is inclined at 45° to the field
The force can never be zero as long as current flows
When the conductor is parallel (0° or 180°) to the magnetic field
explanation: The magnetic force on a conductor of length l carrying current I in field B is given by F = B * I * l * sin(theta). When the conductor is parallel to the field lines (theta = 0° or 180°), sin(theta) = 0, so the force is zero. Force is maximal when perpendicular (theta = 90°).
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.3 Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field

question: What is the crucial role played by the split-ring commutator in a direct-current (DC) electric motor?

It prevents the copper wire from melting due to friction
It provides electrostatic insulation between carbon brushes
It reverses the direction of current in the rotating armature coil every half rotation, maintaining unidirectional torque

subtopic: Field Strength Factors: Solenoid Magnetic Field
question: Which of the following modifications will INCREASE the strength of the magnetic field produced by a cylindrical solenoid?
options: Decreasing the current and removing the iron core
Increasing the number of turns per unit length and increasing the electric current
Unwinding the coil into a straight wire
Substituting an aluminum core for a soft iron core
explanation: The magnetic field inside a solenoid is proportional to the number of turns per unit length (n), the electric current (I), and the permeability of the core material (B = mu * n * I). Increasing the turns, increasing current, or inserting a soft iron core all enhance the field.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.2.3 Magnetic Field due to a Current in a Solenoid

subtopic: Magnetic Pole Behavior: Earth's Magnetic Poles
question: Why does the north-seeking pole (N-pole) of a freely suspended magnetic compass needle point approximately toward the geographic North Pole of Earth?

Earth's rotation pulls compass needles toward the axis of rotation
Earth acts like a giant bar magnet whose magnetic South pole is situated near Earth's geographic North Pole
The solar wind forces all compasses northwards
